title: Convex sets, polyhedra and extreme points

questions.heading: A Polyhedron Is Convex: The Segment Between Two Feasible Points Stays Feasible
questions.stem: A staffing model has continuous variables and rules written as Ax ≤ b. Plans p and q both satisfy every rule. A planner proposes the plan 0.3 p + 0.7 q. What can you say before checking it?

options.text: It may break a rule, since only the midpoint of p and q is guaranteed
options.says: Every point (1 - λ) p + λ q with λ between 0 and 1 is guaranteed, not only λ = 0.5.

options.text: It satisfies every rule, since such a mix of feasible plans stays feasible
options.says: Right: with weights 0.3 and 0.7, A(0.3 p + 0.7 q) = 0.3 Ap + 0.7 Aq ≤ 0.3 b + 0.7 b = b.

options.text: It may break a rule, since a mix is guaranteed only between two vertices
options.says: The argument uses only Ap ≤ b and Aq ≤ b; p and q can be any feasible points.

options.text: It satisfies every rule only when no coefficient of A is negative
options.says: The signs of A do not matter: every set of the form Ax ≤ b is convex.

questions.heading: Extreme Points Are Where Two Rows Are Tight at Once
questions.stem: A model has three continuous variables. At a feasible point exactly two of its rows are tight, and neither row is a multiple of the other. Is the point an extreme point?

options.text: Yes, since the point lies where two independent tight rows meet
options.says: Two tight rows pin down a corner only in two dimensions; in three they meet along a line.

options.text: Yes, since the point is feasible and sits on the region's boundary
options.says: One tight row puts the point on a face of the region, not at a corner.

options.text: No, since a corner in this model needs three independent tight rows
options.says: Right: in n dimensions a vertex needs n linearly independent tight rows, here three.

options.text: No, since a corner needs more rows tight than the model has variables
options.says: A vertex needs n independent tight rows, not all of them; the other rows can have slack.

questions.heading: Yes/No Decisions Break Convexity, and That Is Why Integer Programming Is Hard
questions.stem: A 0/1 model picks among four upgrades. Its LP relaxation, solved by an LP solver, returns the best vertex x = (1, 0.5, 0, 1). What does this say about the best 0/1 plan?

options.text: It is a rounding of that vertex, since the best plan sits beside it
options.says: Nothing places the best plan next to the best vertex; rounding is no fix, as section 3 shows.

options.text: It is that vertex itself, since a linear objective is best at a vertex
options.says: The vertex funds half an upgrade, so it is not a plan; the vertex rule finds the best fractional point.

options.text: It does not exist, since the relaxation's best vertex is fractional
options.says: Every allowed 0/1 plan is still a vertex of the relaxation; it is just not the best one.

options.text: It must be found another way, since the best vertex is not a plan
options.says: Right: plans are corners too, but here a fractional corner wins, so the LP alone does not give the plan.
